(CNN) -- Authorities investigating the case of a boy who disappeared in Kansas almost a decade ago plan to search an undisclosed residence Wednesday, the Butler County sheriff said. An age-progression photo shows what Adam Herrman would like today, as a 21-year-old man. Sheriff Craig Murphy would not disclose details about the residence or why authorities want to search it. He said his department will also search on an area of the Whitewater River, in southern Kansas, on Saturday near where Adam Herrman was last seen. Adam was 11 when he went missing in 1999. He was living in a mobile home park in Towanda, a town about 25 miles northeast of Wichita, with his adoptive parents, Doug and Valerie Herrman, authorities said. Wichita attorney Warner Eisenbise, who is representing Adam's adoptive parents, said the couple believed Adam had run away and didn't report him missing. They "really rue the fact that they didn't" report him missing, he said Monday. A few weeks ago, an undisclosed person contacted the Wichita-Sedgwick County Exploited and Missing Child Unit, expressing concern about Adam, the sheriff said. The Herrmans told Eisenbise that Adam ran away frequently, the attorney said, and they believed he was either with his biological parents or homeless. Although the Herrmans did not report him missing, "they were very worried about him," Eisenbise said. In an interview published Tuesday in The Wichita Eagle, Valerie Herrman said Adam ran away in May 1999 after she spanked him with a belt. She said she was upset but doesn't remember why, The Eagle reported. The couple never reported Adam missing, Valerie Herrman told the paper, because they feared authorities would take Adam and his siblings away because of the spanking. The couple adopted his two younger siblings as well, according to The Eagle. "We love him, and we made a terrible mistake" by not reporting him missing, Doug Herrman told The Eagle. The couple said they searched the mobile home park and other areas for two days after Adam left. "Then we came to the conclusion that the police probably have him, and they're coming to us, probably to get us in trouble," Doug Herrman told the newspaper, but the "police never came." Authorities have searched an empty lot in the Pine Ridge Mobile Home Park where the family lived. There, police found an "answer" to one of their questions, Murphy said Monday without elaborating. Eisenbise said that on December 15, authorities also searched the Herrmans' homes in Derby, outside of Wichita, and took the couple's computer, he said. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children has released an age-progression picture that depicts Adam as he might appear now: a young man with blue eyes and light-colored hair. Adam had been placed in the Herrmans' care when he was about 2, Murphy said Monday. He had been named Irvin Groeninger III when he was born June 8, 1987, Murphy said, and it was not clear when his name was changed. His biological parents relinquished their rights as parents about two decades ago, and Adam and his siblings were put in foster homes, CNN affiliate KWCH reported. "I thought what I was doing for them was in the best interest of the children, and evidently it wasn't," Irvin Groeninger, Adam's biological father,  told KWCH. "If he was still in my custody, this would have never happened." Adam's sister, Tiffany Broadfoot, 22, said she had last seen her brother about 14 years ago at a birthday party. "He had the cutest little round face, little-bitty freckles right up here on the tip of his cheek," she told the station. CNN's Taylor Gandossy contributed to this report.

Law enforcement officials have conducted searches, interviewed family members and acquaintances, and worked to reconstruct the timeline of the boy's final known days. Sheriff's investigators emphasized that the case remains active as they work to determine what happened.

"When a child disappears and no one reports it for years, that fundamentally complicates every aspect of the investigation," a spokesperson for the case noted, underscoring the difficulties faced by the team.

## Questions About the Adoptive Home

The circumstances surrounding Adam's life in the Herrman household have become a focus of scrutiny. Investigators have sought information about the conditions in the home and the nature of the boy's relationship with his adoptive family in the period leading up to his disappearance.

Both adoptive parents have been questioned as part of the ongoing inquiry.

## A Search for Answers

For authorities, the central goal remains determining Adam's fate — whether he is alive somewhere, having run away as claimed, or whether something more sinister occurred.

The case has drawn attention to broader questions about how children in the foster and adoption system can fall through the cracks of oversight, and how a child's absence could go unnoticed by official channels for so long.

# Search for Missing 11-Year-Old Enters Third Week as Questions Mount

*Authorities expand investigation amid family tensions and unanswered questions*

---

**By Staff Reporter**

MAPLE CREEK — Eighteen days after 11-year-old Daniel Reyes-Whitfield was reported missing from his adoptive family's rural home, the search has grown from a local effort into a multi-county investigation, drawing state resources and raising difficult questions about the days leading up to his disappearance.

Daniel was last seen on the evening of October 14, according to the Coldwater County Sheriff's Office, when his adoptive parents say he went to bed in the family's farmhouse off Route 9. By the next morning, they reported, his bedroom was empty and a rear door was found unlocked.

## The Investigation

Sheriff Marcus Bell, who has led the investigation since the initial 911 call, described the case as "the most resource-intensive missing-persons effort this county has undertaken in more than a decade."

"We have canvassed more than 400 acres, deployed K-9 units, and coordinated with state police on aerial searches," Sheriff Bell said at a press conference Thursday. "I want to be clear: this remains an open investigation, and we are not ruling anything out. That includes the possibility that Daniel left on his own, and the possibility that someone helped him leave — or took him."

Pressed by reporters on whether any family members were considered persons of interest, the sheriff was measured.

"We have spoken with everyone in Daniel's life, and everyone has cooperated to varying degrees," he said. "I won't characterize anyone as a suspect. But I will say that timelines matter, and we are working very hard to reconcile some inconsistencies."

The sheriff declined to specify what those inconsistencies were.

## A Family Under Strain

Daniel was adopted three years ago by Robert and Karen Whitfield, following what court records describe as a lengthy termination of parental rights involving his biological father. The circumstances of that adoption have become a central thread in the public conversation surrounding the case.

The Whitfields have not spoken publicly. Instead, they have retained attorney Diane Foster, who issued a statement on their behalf and answered limited questions.

"Robert and Karen are devastated," Foster said. "They have fully cooperated with law enforcement — provided access to their home, submitted to interviews, and handed over Daniel's phone and computer voluntarily. Any suggestion that they are anything other than grieving parents desperate to bring their son home is both false and cruel."

Asked why the family had declined all media interviews, Foster replied: "Because every word they say publicly gets dissected. Their focus is on Daniel, not on defending themselves against internet speculation. They ask only that the public keep sharing his photo and calling the tip line."

## The Biological Father Speaks

Complicating the emotional landscape of the case is the reemergence of Daniel's biological father, Miguel Reyes, who lost his parental rights before the adoption and who has publicly questioned the account offered by the Whitfields.

Reached by phone, Reyes spoke slowly, at times pausing to collect himself.

"I made mistakes when Danny was little. I've never denied that," Reyes said. "I've spent three years trying to get myself right — steady job, my own place. I was working toward asking a court to let me see him again. And now this."

Reyes said investigators had interviewed him twice and that he had provided them with a full accounting of his whereabouts on the night Daniel vanished.

"I've got nothing to hide. I was at work, I clocked in, I clocked out, cameras and all," he said. "I want them to check every part of my life if it helps find my son. But I'll tell you what I keep asking the sheriff: how does an 11-year-old walk out of a locked house in the middle of the night and nobody hears a thing?"

He added: "I'm not accusing anyone of anything. I just want the truth. I want my boy."

Sheriff Bell confirmed that Reyes had been interviewed and said his cooperation had been "consistent," but declined to elaborate.

## A Sibling's Perspective

Perhaps the most poignant voice to emerge has been that of 16-year-old Sofia Whitfield, the couple's older adopted daughter and Daniel's sister, who spoke briefly and with her parents' attorney present.

"Danny wasn't the kind of kid to just run off," Sofia said quietly. "He was scared of the dark. He didn't even like walking to the barn by himself after sunset."

She described her brother as shy, obsessed with dinosaurs, and slow to trust — but fiercely loyal once he did.

"The last thing he said to me was that he was tired and wanted to go to bed early," she recalled. "It doesn't make sense that he would leave. None of it makes sense."

Asked whether there had been any tension in the home, Sofia glanced at Foster before answering.

"Every family has hard days," she said. "But we love him. I just want him to come home so I can tell him that."

## What Comes Next

Investigators have established a dedicated tip line and are reviewing surveillance footage from gas stations and businesses along the highways bordering Coldwater County. Sheriff Bell said several tips have placed a boy matching Daniel's description at locations as far as 60 miles away, though none have been confirmed.

Volunteers continue to gather each morning at the Maple Creek Community Center, organizing ground searches and distributing flyers bearing Daniel's photograph — a gap-toothed smile, brown eyes, a Tyrannosaurus rex on his shirt.

"Somebody knows something," Sheriff Bell said. "A child does not simply vanish. We are asking that person — whoever they are — to search their conscience and pick up the phone."

Daniel Reyes-Whitfield is described as 4-foot-9, approximately 90 pounds, with short brown hair and brown eyes. Anyone with information is urged to contact the Coldwater County Sheriff's Office tip line at (555) 0199-4477. Callers may remain anonymous.

---

*This is a developing story and will be updated as new information becomes available.*
